ideas.name: Difference in pull
ideas.question: Why does the Moon's gravity create tides instead of just moving the whole Earth?
ideas.modelAnswer: Gravity gets weaker with distance, so the near ocean is pulled harder than Earth's centre and the far ocean less. This difference, the tidal force, stretches the Earth instead of just moving it.

whenOptions.text: Explaining why a stretched rubber band differs from a pushed one
Guessing why waves break on the shore
Working out why a kite flies on windy days

ideas.misread: The Moon grabs the sea like a giant straw and slurps it upward, so one big pull does everything!

ideas.name: Two bulges
ideas.question: Why do most coasts get two high tides a day?
ideas.modelAnswer: Stretching the ocean makes two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the far side. Earth spins through both bulges each day, so a beach gets two highs and two lows.

whenOptions.text: Working out why summer is warmer than winter
Predicting how many high tides a beach will have today
Deciding how many meals fit between sunrise and sunset

ideas.misread: The water races around the globe chasing the Moon, so it must sprint past each beach twice!

ideas.name: Later every day
ideas.question: Why does high tide arrive about 50 minutes later each day?
ideas.modelAnswer: While Earth spins, the Moon also moves along its orbit in the same direction. Earth needs about 50 extra minutes to face the Moon again.

whenOptions.text: Planning a beach walk using yesterday's tide time
Choosing when a cake finishes baking
Figuring out why clocks change in spring

ideas.misread: The tide is just lazy and sleeps in a little more every morning, like me!
ideas.sourceTitle: NASA page on the Moon and tides

ideas.name: Spring and neap
ideas.question: Why do tides get bigger and smaller over about two weeks?
ideas.modelAnswer: The Sun makes a smaller tide that adds to or fights the Moon's. At new and full moon they line up for big spring tides, and at quarter moons they clash for gentle neap tides.

whenOptions.text: Choosing the best week for a sailing trip with deep water
Picking spring flowers to plant in the garden
Guessing which day the wind will be strongest

ideas.misread: Spring tides happen only in spring, when the sea springs up like a happy bunny!

ideas.name: Coast shapes tides
ideas.question: Why are tides huge in some places, like the Bay of Fundy, and tiny in others?
ideas.modelAnswer: Funnel-shaped bays squeeze water upward, and a bay whose natural slosh matches the tide gets pushed higher each time. So the local shape of the sea amplifies the same gentle push.

whenOptions.text: Explaining why the Moon looks bigger near the horizon
Explaining why one bay has giant tides and another has tiny ones

script.text: A coast's own shape can boost tides. Funnel-shaped bays squeeze incoming water higher, and a bay that sloshes at the tide's rhythm gets pushed higher each time.
Like pushing a child on a swing at just the right moment, tiny pushes from the Moon build into a huge tide in a narrowing bay.

i1.say: The Moon's pull is stronger on the nearby water and weaker on faraway water, so the uneven pull stretches the Earth rather than just dragging it along.
i1.example: Imagine pulling a piece of taffy with one hand harder than the other: it stretches out long instead of simply sliding across the table.
i1.why: Gravity fades with distance, so the near side, the middle and the far side each feel a slightly different tug from the Moon.
i1.fix: No, the Moon is not a giant straw slurping the sea up with one big pull. The difference in pull across Earth stretches the water.

i2.say: The stretching makes two water bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side, and the spinning Earth carries each beach through both.
i2.example: Standing on a beach for a full day, you would see the water rise high, drop low, rise high again, then drop low again.
i2.why: Because there are two bulges and Earth turns once a day, every coast passes through two high-water spots and two low-water spots.
i2.fix: No, the water does not sprint around the globe chasing the Moon. The bulges stay put while the solid Earth spins through them.

i3.say: The Moon keeps moving along its orbit while Earth turns, so Earth needs about fifty extra minutes to face it again, and tides arrive later each day.
i3.example: If high tide was at 6 am today, expect it to arrive near 6:50 am tomorrow, then around 7:40 the day after.
i3.why: Chasing a moving target takes longer, so a full tidal day lasts a bit more than twenty-four hours.
i3.fix: No, the tide is not lazy or sleeping in. It comes later because the Moon moves ahead and Earth must turn extra to catch up.

i4.say: The Sun adds a smaller tide of its own. When Sun and Moon line up, tides are big; when they pull at right angles, tides are gentle.
i4.example: At full moon or new moon the sea climbs very high and drops very low, but at a half moon the difference is small.
i4.why: Two pulls in the same direction add together, while pulls from different directions partly cancel and make the tidal range smaller.
i4.fix: No, spring tides are not tied to the spring season or a bouncing sea. They happen whenever Sun, Moon and Earth line up, twice every month.

i5.say: A coast's own shape can boost tides. Funnel-shaped bays squeeze incoming water higher, and a bay that sloshes at the tide's rhythm gets pushed higher each time.
i5.example: Like pushing a child on a swing at just the right moment, tiny pushes from the Moon build into a huge tide in a narrowing bay.
i5.why: The Moon's push is the same everywhere, but local geometry and natural sloshing timing decide how much that gentle push is magnified.
i5.fix: No, big tides are not caused by a beach being closer to the Moon. The distance hardly changes; the shape of the bay makes the difference.
